inclusion.rationale: The paper formulates a modular, corpus-estimated word-sequence probability within a factorized speech-decoding objective. It belongs as an engineering integration point on the statistical-ASR branch without being treated as the sole hinge in that broader line of work.

significance.beginner: When speech sounds are ambiguous, the decoder combines how well a candidate matches the sounds with how plausible its word sequence is in the domain.
significance.expert: The maximum-a-posteriori decoder factors Pr(W|A;L) into a language-model probability Pr(W|L) and a front-end likelihood Pr(A|W;L), then searches finite-state hypotheses by likelihood.

limitations: The article specifies a decoder that the IBM group planned to implement; it does not report end-to-end recognition accuracy or an experiment isolating the language-model contribution.
The target is carefully spoken speech in a relatively noiseless environment, with a roughly 10,000-word vocabulary and a two-million-word corpus of laser patent applications.

The decoder begins from a phonetic-symbol string supplied by a separate, speaker-trained acoustic processor rather than learning directly from waveforms; pronunciation and phonological probabilities are also speaker-dependent.
The instantiated language model uses explicit recent-word, part-of-speech, and content-class state features rather than learned distributed representations.
The paper leaves probability estimation for unseen language-model transitions under investigation.

Partial-hypothesis likelihoods use an approximation, and the described decoder scores the best state path while assuming that the loss relative to marginalizing all paths for a word sequence is negligible.
The work concerns speech transcription and does not present the language model as a standalone text generator.

The abstract reports simulations and successful speech-process applications, but the chapter gives no simulation table, dataset specification, quantitative comparison, or recognition metric from which to reconstruct those results.

versions.notes: The official program supplies the scheduled presentation date of 15 August 1986; the proceedings publication itself is dated only to 1986. The eScholarship record’s normalized January date and 2024 repository-ingest date are not treated as publication events. No DOI or open-content license was verified.

inclusion.rationale: The paper supplies a concrete, inspected example in which a network learns internal distributed codes from relational propositions and uses their geometry to generalize within a small structured domain. Bengio et al. later cite this work when describing learned distributed representations for symbolic data. It is retained as a representation-learning precursor, not as a language model or a claim of priority for distributed representations, backpropagation, or modern word vectors.

significance.beginner: Neutral person and relation symbols are translated into learned compact patterns whose similarities reflect useful family-tree regularities, allowing some unseen relations to be completed without hand-written semantic features.
significance.expert: A deterministic feed-forward sigmoid network learns separate six-unit role-specific codes for person and relation inputs, exposes isomorphic family structure in those codes, and tests four withheld relation instances across two random initializations.

limitations: The experiment uses two synthetic isomorphic family trees, 24 people, 12 relation types, and 104 relation instances; four facts are withheld and the same entities, relations, and templates remain in training.

Only two random initializations are reported: one network answers 4 of 4 held-out facts correctly and the other answers 3 of 4. There is no baseline, confidence interval, significance test, or broader held-out study.
The paper describes the chosen layered family-task architecture as somewhat arbitrary and demonstrates only one feasible design, not the best or only design.
The architecture is feed-forward, not recurrent, and its role-specific six-unit codes are not one shared modern word-embedding table.
The word-form analogy is explicitly limited: lexical ambiguity such as bank would require phrase or sentence context that the simulation does not model.
The author says there is no domain-independent prescriptive theory of sensible generalization; the reported result is bounded to particular structured domains.
The learned-unit interpretations are qualitative readings of weights rather than quantitative disentanglement measurements, and sex is omitted from one code because it is redundant for the task.
The family relations encode binary-sex and heteronormative assumptions that require historical contextualization.
The paper calls major aspects of the learning procedure biologically implausible; the paper and complete proceedings have no verified open redistribution license.

inclusion.rationale: The article gives a compact, explicit account of discounting low-count m-grams, reserving probability mass for unseen events, and conditionally falling back to normalized lower-order distributions. It also contrasts this nonlinear backoff construction with Jelinek–Mercer deleted estimation. The work is retained as a classical statistical-language-model branch rather than evidence about neural representation learning or long-context modeling.

significance.beginner: A rare phrase should not consume all the model’s trust, and an m-gram should not be treated as impossible solely because it was absent at the current order. Katz discounts uncertain observed counts, keeps probability in reserve, and uses a broader lower-order pattern when the more specific estimate is zero.
significance.expert: The estimator combines adjusted low-count Turing coefficients, an explicit unseen-mass budget, and a zero-estimate gate that rescales the recursively defined lower-order conditional distribution by α; counts above k are left undiscounted.

limitations: The article is a two-page treatment of an m-gram component for IBM speech recognizers; it does not model distributed representations, semantics, or dependencies beyond the chosen finite context.

The recursion uses a lower order when the higher-order estimate is zero rather than linearly mixing every order; the paper separately reports an optional d₁ = 0 space-saving variant that deliberately makes singleton estimates zero.
The article attributes its frequency-of-frequencies estimator to Turing through Good’s 1953 paper and explicitly locates its own novelty in nonlinear backoff, not in Turing’s formulas.

Table I reports one 100-sentence test on models estimated from approximately 750,000 words of office correspondence, without vocabulary, tokenization, split, uncertainty, or implementation details sufficient for reproduction.
The recommendation that k be about five and the assertion of weak sensitivity to the discount coefficients are practical statements without a displayed sensitivity analysis.
The institutionally hosted scan retains an IEEE copyright line and has no verified open license; it is used for inspection and is not redistributed.

inclusion.rationale: The work connects next-item prediction, carried hidden state, and emergent task-dependent internal structure in inspected sequence experiments. significance.beginner: A copy of the previous hidden pattern lets the same current item produce different predictions after different histories, and learning to predict the next item organizes hidden states without supplying word-class labels.
significance.expert: The architecture copies hidden activation one-for-one through fixed unit-weight links, trains the remaining paths with local next-step error, and reports task-dependent lexical-state geometry and successor-frequency fit on controlled generated sequences.

limitations: The hidden-to-context copy connections are fixed at weight 1.0; only the input/context-to-hidden and hidden-to-output paths are trained. The article does not describe full backpropagation through earlier copied states.

The lexical experiment uses 29 words in 10,000 generated two- and three-word sentences, orthogonal one-hot 31-bit inputs, 150 hidden units plus 150 context units, and six passes; it is not a natural-corpus language-model evaluation.

Network output activations need not sum to one. The reported successor-frequency comparison is not a normalized softmax distribution, likelihood objective, or perplexity evaluation.

Averaging a word’s hidden states across contexts can create a clustering artifact because preceding contexts are category-dependent; the described token-level check is not displayed and has no quantitative clustering metric.
The memory is practically bounded by finite numerical precision, repeated nonlinear transformation, exponential decay, and delayed-error training; representational capacity remains open.

The experiments report no seed count, confidence intervals, recurrence ablation, modern baseline, natural-language-scale syntax test, or reproducible implementation, and the conclusions are described as preliminary.

inclusion.rationale: The work supplies an inspected neural natural-language-processing system in which error-driven learning updates a global distributed word lexicon shared by recurrent modules for sentence-role and scripted-story tasks. Bengio et al. cite it as an earlier neural language-modeling example while explicitly contrasting its word-role objective with their normalized word-sequence distribution. The branch preserves that historical connection without relabeling FGREP or DISPAR as a probabilistic language model.

significance.beginner: Several small recurrent networks learn meaning-like patterns for words in one shared lexicon, then pass those patterns between sentence and story tasks. The system learns expectations and scripted completions, but it does not assign a normalized probability to each possible next word or sentence.
significance.expert: FGREP extends backpropagated error into globally stored input/output word representations, while DISPAR chains four separately supervised recurrent FGREP modules around a shared lexicon. The audited manuscript reports synthetic case-role and script-paraphrase metrics and explicitly frames its probabilistic behavior as weighted-average output patterns rather than an explicit sequence distribution.

limitations: The claim-located reading copy is an author-hosted 46-page prepublication manuscript with internal pp. 1–46, not the publisher’s pp. 343–399 journal layout; technical locators and manuscript-specific wording are not transferred to unseen journal pages.

FGREP and DISPAR learn case-role mappings, paraphrases, and script-conditioned expectation patterns. They do not optimize word-sequence likelihood, normalize a next-word distribution, or report perplexity.
The experiments use generated sentence templates and nine stereotyped restaurant, shopping, and travel story templates rather than a natural text corpus.

The four DISPAR modules are trained separately with compatible intermediate targets; during training, imperfect upstream outputs are replaced by correct patterns from the current lexicon rather than propagated end to end.

An external supervisor supplies fixed role and script slots, module-level targets, sequence segmentation, and execution control. The paper treats automatically discovering intermediate targets and neural control as future work.
The internal representation uses a fixed number of assemblies, cannot naturally represent an unbounded number of fillers, and is optimal only for the task that developed it.

The strong incomplete-story completion behavior depends on low variation and deliberately stereotyped scripts; the authors report poor handling of exceptions and little extrapolation beyond training regularities.
The reported percentages have no confidence intervals, significance tests, repeated-seed analysis, or comparison with a normalized statistical language model.
The publisher record and author-hosted manuscript expose no verified work-level open license; the manuscript is linked for inspection and is not redistributed by this repository.

inclusion.rationale: This work establishes a 1993 node in the atlas’s neural text-compression line. It couples a fixed-window neural next-character estimator to arithmetic coding, reports a held-out newspaper experiment, and explicitly credits collaboration with Stefan Heil. The later two-author family retains the core mechanism while expanding the codec comparison, test design, and evidence, so the 1993 article is modeled as a separate antecedent rather than silently absorbed as a version.

significance.beginner: Before the better-known two-author treatments, this paper already used the previous five characters to predict the next one and let arithmetic coding spend fewer bits on likely characters. It is a separate earlier article, not merely a hidden date attached to the later work.
significance.expert: The article trains an nk-input/k-output feed-forward predictor on one-hot character targets by squared error, sum-normalizes its outputs for arithmetic coding, and reports a 2.68 compression ratio on ten held-out Merkur articles. It frames online learning and recurrent predictors as promising extensions, while its current implementation remains offline and roughly two orders of magnitude slower than conventional methods.

limitations: The inspected artifact is an author-hosted six-leaf PostScript copy with structural anchors rather than stable visible journal folios; no separate publisher full text or DOI was located.

The experiment uses only arithmetic coding with the neural predictor and reports one average compression ratio per method; it gives no variance, confidence interval, significance test, code, learned weights, or public article identities.

The 40 training and 10 test articles come from Münchner Merkur, each stated as 10,000–20,000 characters, but preprocessing, random initialization, training duration, and model-selection details are not supplied.
The network activation, nonnegativity behavior, clipping, zero-probability handling, and finite-precision codec agreement are not specified.
Initial online improvements are qualitative, recurrent predictors are future work, and the reported current offline implementation is about two orders of magnitude slower than conventional methods.

inclusion.rationale: The work gives a concrete fixed-window neural next-character predictor whose estimated probabilities drive synchronized lossless coding, then reports same-newspaper and cross-newspaper compression tests. Bengio et al. later cite it as related character-based neural probability modeling, making it a documented adjacent branch while its squared-error training, post-hoc sum normalization, and coding objective remain distinct from word-level softmax likelihood models.

significance.beginner: A network looks at the previous five characters, estimates what character comes next, and lets a lossless coder spend shorter codes on more likely characters. Because encoder and decoder run the same frozen predictor, the original text can be recovered exactly.
significance.expert: The audited manuscript trains an 80-way fixed-window feed-forward predictor by squared error, sum-normalizes its outputs only during coding, and couples the resulting conditional estimates to Huffman or arithmetic coding. Separate Merkur and Frankenpost tests expose compression gains, transfer degradation, excluded model cost, and severe runtime limits.

limitations: The evaluated network sees only five preceding characters; recurrent networks and longer effective histories are proposed rather than tested.

Squared-error outputs are divided by their sum during coding rather than trained as a softmax likelihood. The activation, nonnegativity guarantee, clipping, and zero-probability handling are not specified.

The 430-hidden-unit network is trained once on unidentified, unreleased newspaper articles and assumed to be preinstalled at both endpoints; its learned weights and training corpus are excluded from each compressed file’s size.

The same-source test uses 20 disjoint Münchner Merkur articles and the transfer test uses 10 Frankenpost articles, without article identities, public splits, confidence intervals, significance tests, seeds, code, or learned weights.
The reported compression ratios are original length divided by compressed length; the paper does not report standard benchmark bits per character or a modern reproducible codec comparison.
The current offline implementation is reported as roughly 1,000 times slower than contemporary standard compressors, and no end-to-end optimized runtime is supplied.
The IEEE version-of-record text was not accessible for claim comparison. Technical evidence uses the author-hosted preprint’s own pagination and is not transferred to journal pp. 142–146.

versions.notes: The RWTH author-group bibliography supplies May 1995 and Detroit as part of the conference citation. The ordering event remains at year precision because that field does not separately establish a proceedings-release month or paper-presentation day. IEEE, the RWTH bibliography, and the printed paper support the 1995 year; IEEE and Crossref confirm the title, abbreviated author order, volume, pages, and DOI. Crossref’s null issued date and later DOI-deposit date are not publication dates.

inclusion.rationale: The paper makes the lower-order distribution itself an object of estimation for unseen m-grams. Its distinct-context and singleton-count solutions explain why raw lower-order frequency can be a poor fallback signal and provide a major classical backoff node; the later interpolated and modified variants are recorded as a separate, sourced extension.

significance.beginner: A word that is frequent in only a few fixed phrases should not automatically look likely after every unseen context. The fallback distribution asks how broadly a word continues different contexts, not only how often it appears.
significance.expert: The paper preserves a normalized seen/unseen backoff form and optimizes its lower-order distribution in two ways: the marginal-constraint path yields distinct-context counts under absolute discounting, while a separate leave-one-out path yields singleton-event counts.

limitations: The paper is a four-page ICASSP treatment whose main Verbmobil and Wall Street Journal comparisons use trigram language models; its final ARPA comparison adds one bigram row, and it does not model distributed representations, semantics, or long context.

The marginal derivation treats the denominator in equation (6) as constant with respect to the predicted word, and the leave-one-out derivation makes an analogous approximation to the second sum in equation (16).
The simple distinct-context result assumes nested history classes, reliable coarse marginals, one unique coarser class for each detailed history, and a single absolute discount with 0 < d < 1.

The experiments use nonlinear interpolation from Ney, Essen, and Kneser 1994 as a slight variant of absolute discounting for seen events, and smooth every backoff distribution by an unspecified method to avoid zero probabilities.

The paper does not present the later interpolated Kneser–Ney formulation or modified Kneser–Ney’s count-dependent D₁, D₂, and D₃₊ discounts; the separate Chen–Goodman record must not be projected backward into its equations.
The abstract’s claim of perplexity improvements up to about 10% is approximate: Table 1’s compact marginal-constraint row changes from 169.4 to 150.6, an 11.1% relative reduction.
The reported 5% word-error improvement is an approximate relative summary, not a five-percentage-point reduction: the best full WSJ row changes from 11.9% to 11.1%.
No significance analysis, confidence interval, runtime benchmark, measured memory footprint, discount-tuning procedure, complete preprocessing description, or test-set size is reported.
The institutionally hosted PDF retains an IEEE copyright line and provides no explicit open license; it is used for inspection and is not redistributed.

uncertainties.resolutionCondition: Inspect an authoritative ICASSP 1995 program or session schedule identifying the paper’s presentation.

versions.notes: MIT Press supplies the canonical title, authors, issue, journal pagination, article history, publication date, DOI, and a displayed © 1997 Massachusetts Institute of Technology notice. The institutionally hosted reading copy is a complete 32-page author-layout PDF; its stable internal pages support claim location but never map to journal pp. 1735–1780.

inclusion.rationale: The report versions and journal article isolate exponentially unstable or decaying temporal error flow, construct a unit-weight recurrent state path, and regulate storage and access with learned multiplicative gates. This supplies the recurrent-memory branch later applied to word language modeling, while its evidence remains bounded to artificial long-lag tasks and its cell predates the learned forget gate and cell-state-to-gate connections used in later systems.

significance.beginner: A memory cell keeps one internal value on a fixed recurrent loop, while learned input and output gates decide when new information may enter and when stored information may affect the network. This makes long-delayed learning signals easier to preserve, but it does not make every long-memory problem easy.
significance.expert: The architecture creates a constant error carousel through a unit-weight self-connection, learns multiplicative input and output gates, and uses a spatially and temporally local truncated-gradient algorithm. Its synthetic experiments include minimal lags above 1,000 steps, while the discussion preserves delayed-XOR, parity, capacity, counting, and parameter-overhead boundaries.

limitations: All reported experiments use generated artificial sequences; speech processing, time-series prediction, and music are future applications rather than evaluated evidence.

The efficient algorithm deliberately truncates error flow when it leaves memory cells or gate units. The paper says strongly delayed XOR-like tasks may require a full gradient, while also reporting that its few non-truncated trials did not materially differ.
Table 3’s thousand-step results concern a two-class trigger-and-distractor task with error only at sequence ends, not natural language, continuous discourse, or real-world memory.
Each memory-cell block adds input and output gate units. The discussion bounds dense-network weight overhead and notes capacity, precise counting, parity, and internal-state-drift problems.
The original cell has input and output gates but no learned forget gate or cell-state-to-gate feedback links; those later modifications must not be projected backward into this work.
The inspected report versions and journal text provide no code or code link, learned parameters, data generator package, hardware-normalized timing, or modern replication protocol.

The MIT record displays © 1997 Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and the original report’s series notice asks that reports not be copied. The linked reading copies are not redistributed by this repository.

uncertainties.note: The 21 August 1995 original report, December 1996 version 3.0 revision, and 15 November 1997 journal article remain distinct versions and chronology events; the work is ordered by the original report without backdating either later version.

The original architecture exposes input and output gates only. Learned forget gates and cell-state-to-gate connections belong to later publications and enter the corpus only through the bounded 2012 variant claim.

inclusion.rationale: The expanded report turns the continuation-based lower-order distribution into an explicitly interpolated recursive estimator, adds separate discounts for one-, two-, and three-or-more-count n-grams, and evaluates those choices across multiple corpora, training sizes, and n-gram orders. significance.beginner: In the tested implementations, two separate choices can improve a count model: simpler continuation patterns can still contribute when a longer phrase has been seen, and phrases seen once, twice, or at least three times need not surrender the same amount of probability.
significance.expert: The report recasts the Kneser–Ney continuation distribution as recursive interpolation, assigns per-order D₁, D₂, and D₃₊ discounts, distinguishes held-out, fixed-count, and hard-backoff variants, and evaluates those implementation choices under a broad cross-entropy protocol.

limitations: The work studies smoothing for count-based word n-gram models, chiefly bigrams and trigrams; it does not model distributed representations, neural parameter sharing, semantics, or long context.

The same-title 1996 ACL paper reports an earlier comparison and two different smoothing methods but contains no Kneser–Ney treatment. It is prior research, not a version of this modified-Kneser–Ney record, and the contribution is ordered at the August 1998 report.

The fixed D₁, D₂, and D₃₊ equations are attributed to Klaus Ries through personal communication. The journal version also says Ney, Martin, and Wessel 1997 independently used two discounts, so the corpus makes no sole-priority claim about multiple discounts.

The strongest comparisons are bounded to the authors’ implementations, four English corpora, tested training sizes, word n-gram orders, held-out procedures, and cross-entropy metric; they are not universal superiority claims.

Many conditions are shown as curves without confidence intervals or p-values. The report warns that single-run variation can be comparable to roughly one-percent perplexity differences and recommends repeated runs where possible.

The authors’ `kneser-ney` baseline recursively smooths lower orders and tunes a separate discount at each order on held-out data. Its reported performance must not be attributed to the exact hard-backoff estimator printed in Kneser and Ney 1995.
The count-estimated fixed variant avoids held-out optimization but depends on count-of-counts values n₁ through n₄ and generally performs slightly worse in the reported comparisons.

versions.notes: The canonical citation follows the DOI deposit and institutional journal record. The IEEE article appears to be a fuller treatment of the NIPS conference paper because the mechanism, abstract, datasets, and table structure closely overlap, but no inspected primary record explicitly labels one an extension of the other.

inclusion.rationale: The work supplies the explicitly cited neural joint-distribution mechanism that the later neural probabilistic language model adapts: an ordered product of conditional distributions whose constrained hidden units share computation across predictions. Its separate NIPS, IDIAP, and IEEE records preserve the 1999 conference event and distinct 2000 publication artifacts without treating bibliographic suffixes as chronology or asserting a direction among the companion treatments.

significance.beginner: A huge table of every possible variable combination becomes a sequence of smaller questions. A constrained neural network answers those questions while reusing hidden features, so evidence from observed combinations can inform combinations the data did not contain.
significance.expert: The model applies an order-sensitive chain factorization, parameterizes normalized conditionals with triangular grouped connectivity and shared deterministic hidden units, grows as O(n²H) under its stated construction, and trains by likelihood or MAP; its pruning rule and four-dataset likelihood study expose both the intended capacity control and its empirical limits.

limitations: The model operates on fixed-dimensional vectors of variables; it does not itself implement variable-length language modeling or time-shared next-word prediction.
The variable order is chosen rather than learned, and the approximation can change when that order changes.
General marginalization can require a combinatorial sum; missing values are tractable only in restricted cases described by the authors.
The connectivity-pruning procedure uses pairwise Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests and a cross-validated threshold, so it is a heuristic rather than a search over all higher-order dependencies.

ideas.name: Entropy as sequence uncertainty
ideas.description: Conditional entropy quantifies average uncertainty about a next event when contextual information is known.

ideas.description: The rank frequencies of next-character predictions can be related to upper and lower bounds on conditional entropy.

ideas.name: Language-model-guided decoding
ideas.description: A decoder can rank candidate word sequences by combining their language-model probability with the likelihood of the observed signal.

ideas.name: Corpus-estimated language model
ideas.description: A structured sequence model can obtain transition probabilities from counts over a domain corpus.

ideas.name: Sparse language-model estimation
ideas.description: A finite sample can leave plausible sequence transitions with zero observed or expected counts, so an estimated probability of zero need not mark an impossible transition.

ideas.name: Interpolated transition estimation
ideas.description: A transition estimate can blend a detailed distribution with a more broadly tied distribution, with the mixing weight reflecting their relative reliability.

ideas.name: Deleted estimation

ideas.name: Frequency-of-frequencies discounting
ideas.description: Counts of how many event types occur once, twice, and so on can adjust unreliable low counts and estimate how much total probability should remain for unseen events.

uncertainties.note: Katz attributes the adjusted-count estimator to Turing through Good’s 1953 paper; the corpus does not treat it as Katz’s invention.

ideas.name: Recursive m-gram backoff
ideas.description: A higher-order m-gram model can use a seen-event estimate directly and send unseen events to a normalized lower-order distribution. Katz makes that estimator recursive with an explicit reserved-mass calculation; Kneser and Ney preserve the seen/unseen structure while redesigning the fallback distribution.

uncertainties.note: In Katz’s estimator, this is a zero-estimate gate, not interpolation across all orders; α rescales the lower-order distribution over eligible unseen continuations to the reserved mass β̃ rather than acting as a convex mixture weight.

The papers reuse Greek letters for different quantities: Katz’s α is a lower-order multiplier and β̃ is reserved mass, whereas Kneser and Ney’s α is the seen-event estimate, β is the fallback distribution, and γ is its normalizer.

ideas.name: Context-diversity backoff distributions
ideas.description: A lower-order distribution can depend on how many distinct detailed contexts contain the observed continuation, or on how many such context–continuation events are singletons, rather than on the continuation’s raw token frequency. The original paper uses it for backoff; later work also interpolates it into seen-event estimates.

uncertainties.note: The distinct-context equation is the original paper’s marginal-constraint backoff distribution; later interpolated and modified Kneser–Ney estimators add mechanisms not present in this record.

ideas.name: Interpolated Kneser–Ney smoothing
ideas.description: A discounted higher-order n-gram estimate is recursively added to a scaled continuation-based lower-order distribution for every continuation, so lower-order evidence contributes to both seen and unseen events.

uncertainties.note: Interpolation is a later formulation: the 1995 Kneser–Ney paper applies its optimized lower-order distribution through a seen/unseen backoff gate.

ideas.name: Modified Kneser–Ney count-dependent discounts
ideas.description: Each n-gram order can use separate absolute discounts for events observed once, twice, and three or more times, with the interpolation weight returning the total removed mass through the continuation distribution.

uncertainties.note: The three discount tiers, interpolation choice, and parameter-estimation choice remain separate properties; “modified Kneser–Ney” must not be reduced to any one of them.
The fixed three-discount equations cite Klaus Ries through personal communication, and the journal article reports an independent two-discount proposal by Ney, Martin, and Wessel 1997.

ideas.name: Neural factorization of joint distributions
ideas.description: An ordered product of normalized conditional distributions is parameterized by a constrained neural network whose deterministic hidden units can share computation across several conditionals.

uncertainties.note: The hidden units are deterministic shared computations, not latent random variables; normalization comes from the product of normalized conditionals.

The precursor’s suggestion to represent large-domain values such as words with low-dimensional features is not treated as an implemented language model or as priority evidence for jointly learned word embeddings.

ideas.name: Low-dimensional feature encoding for large domains
ideas.description: Values of a large categorical domain can be represented through multiple low-dimensional features before applying a joint-distribution estimator; in the audited precursor this is a proposal for text, not an implemented or learned representation.

uncertainties.note: The record preserves the paper’s proposed encoding bridge without treating it as experimental language-model evidence or as priority evidence for learned word representations.

ideas.name: Jointly learned word representations
ideas.description: A shared lookup table maps each word type to a continuous vector, and those vectors are optimized together with the probability model rather than supplied as fixed external features.

uncertainties.note: The paper describes learned continuous word features and distributed representations; the atlas uses modern embedding terminology only as explanatory interface language, not as a quotation or priority claim.

ideas.name: Fixed-window feed-forward neural language modeling
ideas.description: A feed-forward network predicts the next word from a fixed window of shared word vectors, optionally combining a nonlinear hidden path with a direct input-to-output path.

ideas.name: Full-vocabulary neural normalization
ideas.description: One score per vocabulary item is exponentiated and normalized into a next-word distribution, coupling every training example to the full output vocabulary.

uncertainties.note: Mikolov et al. normalize retained word types plus one rare-word bucket, then divide that bucket’s probability uniformly among the merged rare types; this is not one separately learned output for every original rare type.

ideas.name: Class-factored neural output normalization
ideas.description: A word probability is decomposed into the probability of its assigned class and its probability within that class, reducing the number of output scores evaluated for each history.

uncertainties.note: The 2012 paper evaluates fixed word classes and discusses the square-root class-count heuristic; this idea does not imply a learned hierarchy or a modern approximate-softmax method.

ideas.name: Shortlist hybrid neural language modeling
ideas.description: A neural distribution is normalized over a frequent-word shortlist and scaled by the backoff model’s total shortlist mass, while the backoff model retains the remaining vocabulary probability.

uncertainties.note: The selected system is not a fixed linear mixture across the full vocabulary: it preserves a history-dependent shortlist mass taken from the backoff model.

ideas.name: Context-cached neural language-model decoding
ideas.description: When a decoder sequentially requests many word probabilities for the same history, the outputs already produced by one neural forward pass can be reused across those requests.

ideas.name: Neural and count-model mixtures
ideas.description: A neural next-word distribution can be linearly mixed with an interpolated n-gram distribution so their different generalization behavior contributes to one normalized predictor.

uncertainties.note: The evidence is paper-specific: Bengio et al. use fixed equal-weight neural/interpolated-trigram mixtures; Mikolov et al. report RNN/backoff weights of 0.75/0.25 plus RNN ensembles; and Sundermeyer et al. separately tune a Kneser–Ney/LSTM interpolation whose components use more than four billion versus 27 million training words. None of these results implies that mixtures always improve either component.

ideas.name: Learned distributed representations for symbols
ideas.description: A system can learn multi-unit internal patterns for otherwise discrete symbols so task-relevant regularities are encoded across several units rather than supplied as hand-written symbolic features.

uncertainties.note: This shared idea records a broad representation principle. It does not equate Hinton’s role-specific family codes, Elman’s context-dependent hidden states, Miikkulainen and Dyer’s task-learned global word-type patterns, and Bengio’s static jointly learned word lookup rows.

ideas.name: Similarity-based generalization in learned representation space
ideas.description: Learned internal geometry can expose task-relevant similarities so a model’s behavior transfers among structurally related cases rather than depending only on exact symbolic identity.

uncertainties.note: The Hinton evidence is restricted to two small isomorphic family graphs and four withheld facts; it is not broad semantic or cross-domain transfer evidence.

The Miikkulainen–Dyer evidence is restricted to supervised case-role and stereotyped script tasks; its similarity and cloning results do not establish portable word semantics or open-domain generalization.

ideas.name: Simple recurrent context memory
ideas.description: A copy of the previous hidden activation is supplied as context for the next step, making current state and output depend jointly on the current input and an iterated summary of prior processing.

uncertainties.note: The copied hidden-to-context links are fixed at 1.0; this idea must not be rendered as though every recurrent connection is learned or the paper trained with full backpropagation through time.
Miikkulainen and Dyer explicitly reuse Elman-style copied context, but recurrent FGREP predicts a stationary case-role target rather than the next word.

ideas.name: Constant-error recurrent memory
ideas.description: A recurrent cell preserves internal state and backward error along a fixed unit-weight self-connection, creating a path that avoids exponential decay or growth while that path remains active.

uncertainties.note: A protected error path is a local architectural property, not a guarantee that training will learn arbitrary long-range dependencies; both promoted works retain explicit task and evidence limits.

ideas.name: Gated recurrent memory access
ideas.description: Learned multiplicative controls regulate whether candidate information enters recurrent state and whether stored state affects cell output; later variants add a learned control over state retention.

uncertainties.note: The 1995/1997 version has input and output gates only; the 2012 implementation also uses a later forget gate and cell-state-to-gate connections, which are not attributed backward.

ideas.name: Task-learned global distributed word lexicon
ideas.description: Backpropagated task error can update one stored distributed pattern per word and reuse that shared pattern as input, output, and inter-module communication across several supervised language-processing tasks.

uncertainties.note: The stored word pattern is global within DISPAR, but its geometry is learned for the supervised tasks and is not a context-dependent token representation or a word vector trained by language-model likelihood.

ideas.name: Modular recurrent neural language processing
ideas.description: Several recurrent networks can specialize in sentence parsing, story parsing, story generation, and sentence generation while communicating through a compatible learned lexicon and explicit case-role or script structures.

uncertainties.note: The modules are separately supervised with compatible targets and correct intermediate lexical patterns during training; the corpus does not describe DISPAR as an end-to-end learned pipeline.

ideas.name: One-hot neural bigram language modeling
ideas.description: A one-hot current-word input can feed a full-vocabulary affine softmax directly, making the network a normalized bigram estimator with no hidden representation and no context beyond one word.

uncertainties.note: The evaluated system contains no hidden units or learned word vectors; calling it neural records its optimization and softmax parameterization, not distributed representation learning.

ideas.name: Early stopping as implicit neural bigram smoothing
ideas.description: Selecting a direct bigram network before full training convergence can regularize sparse word-pair estimates; an exact count-dependent interpolation is derived only for a separate linear squared-error surrogate, while the actual softmax network's smoothing form remains unknown.

uncertainties.note: The corpus does not transfer equations (5.1)–(5.3) from the linear, no-bias, squared-error analysis to the implemented softmax likelihood model.

ideas.name: Next-item prediction as a training task
ideas.description: The observed next element supplies a local target, and pressure to predict it can make hidden state encode regularities in the preceding sequence.

uncertainties.note: For Elman’s lexical experiment this objective uses unnormalized output activations on generated sentences; it is not a softmax language-model likelihood or perplexity objective.
Mikolov et al. instantiate the next-word objective as a normalized vocabulary distribution trained with cross-entropy, but propagate only the current-step error in the main experiments.

ideas.name: Recurrent neural word language modeling
ideas.description: A recurrent hidden state combines the current word with the previous state to parameterize a normalized next-word distribution, allowing history to enter through repeated state updates rather than an explicit fixed window.

uncertainties.note: Recurrence removes an explicit finite input window but does not guarantee usable long-range memory; the target paper explicitly reports that its simple model did not capture truly long context.

ideas.name: Online neural language-model adaptation
ideas.description: A trained neural language model can continue stochastic-gradient updates while processing an ordered test sequence, adapting its parameters to recent text in a cache-like continuous space.

uncertainties.note: The method assumes locally coherent test order; the paper’s WSJ evaluation sentences are not consecutive, and its dynamic model is worse than the static model on that split.

ideas.name: Emergent contextual lexical structure
ideas.description: Hidden states induced by prediction over controlled word sequences can cluster by generator-defined lexical roles even though the input vectors themselves carry no category or meaning labels.

uncertainties.note: The plotted type averages can reflect category-dependent preceding contexts; the paper’s described token-level check is not displayed and supplies no quantitative cluster metric.
